Reading

The innocent reading first, and it holds for the frame. Asked the title, the Overview names the paper's makers as heteronyms of Lee Sharks, gives the deposit date, the venue and the epigraph (Rev 4:8, whose order ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ὢν the record prints), states the turnabout of the title, and names the four powers in the record's order. It is attributed. Read against the record, five things move. (1) The charge is quoted with a word the record lacks: 'proposes a source relation that the physical evidence does not show' against the record's 'proposes a source relation the evidence does not show'. (2) The four powers are glossed loosely: presupposition as degree ('how heavily … assumed') where the record has entry as a premise without prior proof; text as 'assumed stability' where the record has 'a wording, an apparatus and an edition'; candidacy as 'viability to act as an explanatory root' where the record has admission 'wherever a source is sought'. Assignment is near. (3) Revelation First is framed from outside, 'a minority position' on 'the Book of Revelation (or a core layer of it)'; neither phrase is in the record, and the core layer is foreign to it. (4) The synoptic problem is made the paper's target, where the record 'leaves the synoptic problem undecided' and audits the allocation of status. (5) The existing text is left plural and unnamed, 'tangible, existing texts', where the title's 'the One That Exists' names the Apocalypse. The centre is absent: Hitzig's reading of Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 (1843, 'einen zwingenden Beweis'), the five critics after him, the source theories that never admitted it, the census of 2.53 million words, the Feist comparison. The stratum from Lachmann to Streeter appears only as 'Q'.

Findings
  • COMPOSED FROM THE RESOLVER. Six of the body's citations are one redirect, carded as 'AXN:0C29.GENERATIVE. — Alexanarch AXN resolver'; the record page /s/records/1746/ is not carded. A second redirect is cited once, beside it, with Wikipedia's 'Biblical criticism' the other card.
  • A WORD INSIDE THE QUOTATION. 'proposes a source relation that the physical evidence does not show' against the record's 'The charge Revelation First meets is that it proposes a source relation the evidence does not show.' The added 'physical' is set inside quotation marks.
  • THE POWERS GLOSSED. Record: (a) Presupposition: it may enter an argument as a premise without first being proven.; (b) Assignment: material in other texts may be assigned to it.; (c) Text: it may be given a wording, an apparatus and an edition.; (d) Candidacy: it is admitted as a candidate wherever a source is sought. Composition: 1. Presupposition: How heavily the existence of the source is assumed in subsequent arguments. 2. Assignment: How confidently specific verses or fragments are credited to the source. 3. Text: The assumed stability of the source's wording despite having no physical manuscript. 4. Candidacy: The text’s viability to act as an explanatory root for other surviving works.
  • FRAMED FROM OUTSIDE. 'The Target: The paper addresses the "Revelation First" hypothesis—a minority position proposing that the Book of Revelation (or a core layer of it) holds a chronological or structural precedence in source relations.' Neither 'minority' nor 'core layer' is in the record; the record 'leaves the synoptic problem undecided'.
  • THE ONE THAT EXISTS UNNAMED. The body has 'than tangible, existing texts that are sidelined by alternative source hypotheses'; the record: 'The title keeps "the One That Exists", which names the Apocalypse.'
  • THE CENTRE ABSENT. 'In 1843 Hitzig argued from Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 that Matthew used the Apocalypse, calling the passage "einen zwingenden Beweis"', the critics after him, and 'A frozen census of 2.53 million words of seated Greek measures what the commentators did not': none composed.
  • LAG (operator, 2026-11-11 00:57 EST): deposited 2026-11-06; one composition signed in, then four immediate attempts without one, then this composition in incognito, five days after deposit. Retrieval at this address is unstable.

[1] Deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on November 6, 2026, the paper was written for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics and features Revelation 4:8 as its epigraph. [1] The Core Argument The paper enters a niche but fiercely debated niche in New Testament source criticism, specifically taking aim at how mainstream biblical scholarship evaluates lost or hypothetical source texts (like the Q source) compared to surviving canonical texts. [1] * The Target: The paper addresses the "Revelation First" hypothesis—a minority position proposing that the Book of Revelation (or a core layer of it) holds a chronological or structural precedence in source relations. [1] * The "I Know You Are" Turnabout: Mainstream biblical criticism frequently dismisses the Revelation First model by claiming it "proposes a source relation that the physical evidence does not show". Sharks (writing as Sigil and Cranes) flips this accusation back on the academic establishment. [1] * The Hypothetical vs. The Real: The paper conducts an audit of the Q source (the universally discussed, entirely hypothetical collection of Jesus's sayings used to explain the Synoptic Problem). It argues that mainstream biblical criticism has ironically granted a completely missing text (Q) a far more robust, uncontested "evidentiary status" in academic discourse than tangible, existing texts that are sidelined by alternative source hypotheses. [[1], [2]] The Framework of Evidentiary Status To prove how a phantom text achieved higher authority than an existing one, the paper analyzes the source arguments through four specific linguistic and forensic powers: 1. Presupposition: How heavily the existence of the source is assumed in subsequent arguments. 2. Assignment: How confidently specific verses or fragments are credited to the source. 3. Text: The assumed stability of the source's wording despite having no physical manuscript. 4. Candidacy: The text’s viability to act as an explanatory root for other surviving works. [1] If you are tracking the broader work of Lee Sharks or the Revelation First debate, let me know if you would like to explore how Q became the dominant paradigm or look closely at the semiotic framework used in the paper.
